title: Hedging in Academic Writing
text:
In academic writing, authors rarely state claims with absolute certainty. Instead, they often use hedges such as 'may', 'appear to', or 'tends to' to signal that a finding is provisional. Such language protects the writer from overstating results that future studies might contradict. Readers, in turn, learn to treat hedged statements as tentative rather than conclusive.

Hedging is not merely a sign of weakness, however. A carefully placed qualifier can show intellectual honesty and invite constructive debate. Conversely, a writer who hedges too heavily may seem evasive, undermining confidence in their own argument. Skilled writers therefore calibrate their certainty, reserving boldness for claims that the evidence strongly supports.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, why do authors use hedges?
options: To signal that a finding is provisional
To make claims sound more dramatic
To avoid citing any previous research
To guarantee that results are permanent

questions.text: What does the second paragraph say a writer who hedges too heavily may seem?
What can be inferred about how readers should interpret a hedged statement?
options: As a claim that still requires further evidence
As a proven and final conclusion
As a deliberate attempt to mislead
As a claim the author has no opinion on

questions.text: Which principle does the passage imply that skilled writers follow?
options: Matching the strength of their language to the strength of the evidence
Avoiding all qualifiers to appear more authoritative
Using hedges uniformly across every sentence
Letting readers decide without offering any stance

vocabulary.definition: expressions that qualify a claim to show uncertainty
avoiding a direct answer or a clear commitment
to adjust something precisely to match a particular standard

paragraph_translations: Na escrita acadêmica, os autores raramente afirmam suas conclusões com certeza absoluta. Em vez disso, costumam usar ressalvas como 'may', 'appear to' ou 'tends to' para sinalizar que um resultado é provisório. Essa linguagem protege o autor de exagerar resultados que estudos futuros podem contradizer. Os leitores, por sua vez, aprendem a tratar afirmações com ressalvas como tentativas, e não como conclusões definitivas.

No entanto, a ressalva não é apenas um sinal de fraqueza. Um qualificador bem colocado pode demonstrar honestidade intelectual e abrir espaço para um debate construtivo. Por outro lado, um autor que usa ressalvas em excesso pode parecer evasivo, o que enfraquece a confiança em seu próprio argumento. Por isso, escritores habilidosos calibram sua certeza, reservando a ousadia para afirmações que a evidência sustenta com firmeza.
